title: Equivalent Trigonometric Expressions
overview: Different-looking trigonometric expressions can have exactly the same value for every angle. In this section you will discover the **cofunction identities** using right triangles and further identities using rotations and reflections on the unit circle, then use them to evaluate expressions, find angles and simplify formulas.
objectives: Derive the cofunction identities from a right triangle.
Use transformations of the unit circle to derive identities for $\frac{\pi}{2}\pm x$, $\pi\pm x$, $\frac{3\pi}{2}\pm x$ and $2\pi - x$.
Use equivalent expressions to evaluate trig ratios and determine unknown angles.
Verify equivalence with graphing technology and explain why graphs are not proof.
Apply equivalent expressions to simplify formulas in applications.

lessons.title: Equivalent expressions and identities
lessons.body:
Two trigonometric expressions are **equivalent** if they give the same value for every angle where both are defined. An equation stating that two expressions are equivalent is a **trigonometric identity**.

You already know some identities:

| Type | Identities |
|---|---|
| Reciprocal | $\csc x = \frac{1}{\sin x}$, $\sec x = \frac{1}{\cos x}$, $\cot x = \frac{1}{\tan x}$ |
| Quotient | $\tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}$, $\cot x = \frac{\cos x}{\sin x}$ |
| Pythagorean | $\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1$ |

The Pythagorean identity comes from the unit circle: the point $(\cos x, \sin x)$ is 1 unit from the origin, so $x^2 + y^2 = 1$.

In this section you will build a new family: identities that relate trig functions of $x$ to trig functions of $\frac{\pi}{2} \pm x$, $\pi \pm x$, $\frac{3\pi}{2} \pm x$ and $2\pi - x$.

**Seeing equivalence on a graph:** if two expressions are equivalent, their graphs lie exactly on top of each other.

```plot
title: y = sin x (solid) and y = cos(π/2 − x) (dashed) are the same curve
f: sin(x) | label=y = sin x
f: cos(pi/2 - x) | dashed; label=y = cos(π/2 − x)
domain: -6.3, 6.3
range: -1.5, 1.5
xticks: pi
```

lessons.title: Cofunction identities (complementary angles)
lessons.body:
In right triangle $ABC$ with the right angle at $B$, if $\angle A = x$ then $\angle C = \frac{\pi}{2} - x$ (the angles add to $\pi$). The two acute angles are **complementary**.

The side opposite $A$ is adjacent to $C$, so

$$\sin x = \frac{a}{b} = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right).$$

Doing this for all six ratios gives the **cofunction identities**:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| $\sin x = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)$ | $\cos x = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)$ | $\tan x = \cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)$ |
| $\csc x = \sec\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)$ | $\sec x = \csc\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)$ | $\cot x = \tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)$ |

**Why "co"?** *Co*sine is the sine of the *co*mplementary angle. Each function is paired with its co-function: sin–cos, tan–cot, sec–csc.

**Quick test:** $\sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac12$ and $\cos\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac12$. Indeed $\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{6}$.

lessons.title: Identities from the unit circle: rotating by π/2
lessons.body:
Put $P(\cos x, \sin x)$ on the unit circle. Rotating $P$ by $\frac{\pi}{2}$ counterclockwise sends a point $(a, b)$ to $(-b, a)$. The new point $P'$ is at angle $x + \frac{\pi}{2}$:

$$P' = \left(\cos\left(x + \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right), \sin\left(x + \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right) = (-\sin x, \cos x).$$

Matching coordinates gives

$$\cos\left(x + \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = -\sin x,\qquad \sin\left(x + \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \cos x,\qquad \tan\left(x + \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = -\cot x.$$

The textbook also writes these as $\sin\left(x - \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = -\cos x$ and $\cos\left(x - \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \sin x$ (rotate clockwise instead).

lessons.title: Identities with π, 3π/2 and 2π
lessons.body:
Use symmetry on the unit circle, with $x$ a first-quadrant angle and $P(\cos x, \sin x)$.

| Angle | Geometry | Point | Resulting identities |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\pi - x$ | reflect $P$ in the $y$-axis | $(-\cos x, \sin x)$ | $\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x$, $\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos x$, $\tan(\pi - x) = -\tan x$ |
| $\pi + x$ | rotate $P$ by $\pi$ | $(-\cos x, -\sin x)$ | $\sin(\pi + x) = -\sin x$, $\cos(\pi + x) = -\cos x$, $\tan(\pi + x) = \tan x$ |
| $2\pi - x$ | reflect $P$ in the $x$-axis | $(\cos x, -\sin x)$ | $\sin(2\pi - x) = -\sin x$, $\cos(2\pi - x) = \cos x$, $\tan(2\pi - x) = -\tan x$ |
| $\frac{3\pi}{2} - x$ | | $(-\sin x, -\cos x)$ | $\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} - x\right) = -\cos x$, $\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} - x\right) = -\sin x$ |
| $\frac{3\pi}{2} + x$ | | $(\sin x, -\cos x)$ | $\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} + x\right) = -\cos x$, $\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} + x\right) = \sin x$ |

**A memory strategy (no table needed):**
1. With $\pi$ or $2\pi$, the function **stays the same** (sin stays sin). With $\frac{\pi}{2}$ or $\frac{3\pi}{2}$, it **switches to the cofunction**.
2. The **sign** is the sign of the *original* function in the quadrant where the angle lands, pretending $x$ is a small first-quadrant angle.

*Example:* $\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} - x\right)$: $\frac{3\pi}{2}$ → switch to sine. The angle $\frac{3\pi}{2} - x$ lands in quadrant III, where cosine is negative. So $\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} - x\right) = -\sin x$.

The reciprocal functions follow the same pattern as their partners.

lessons.title: Using equivalent expressions
lessons.body:
**1. Evaluate one ratio from another.** Given $\sin\frac{\pi}{5}\approx 0.5878$, find $\cos\frac{3\pi}{10}$:

$\frac{3\pi}{10} = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{5}$, so $\cos\frac{3\pi}{10} = \sin\frac{\pi}{5}\approx 0.5878$.

And $\cos\frac{7\pi}{10}$: $\frac{7\pi}{10} = \frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{5}$, so $\cos\frac{7\pi}{10} = -\sin\frac{\pi}{5}\approx -0.5878$.

**2. Find an unknown angle.** If $\csc a = \sec 1.45$ with $a$ in quadrant I, the cofunction identity $\csc a = \sec\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - a\right)$ tells us $\frac{\pi}{2} - a = 1.45$, so $a = \frac{\pi}{2} - 1.45\approx 0.12$.

**3. Solve for angles in arguments.** If $\sec a = \csc 3a$, the arguments of a cofunction pair add to $\frac{\pi}{2}$: $a + 3a = \frac{\pi}{2}$, so $a = \frac{\pi}{8}$.

**4. Simplify formulas.** The banking-turn formula $r = \frac{v^2}{g}\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right)$ becomes $r = \frac{v^2}{g}\cot\theta = \frac{v^2}{g\tan\theta}$.

**5. Check with technology.** Graph both sides; identical graphs support (but do not prove) equivalence.

keyTerms.definition: Expressions that have equal values for every angle at which both are defined.
An equation involving trigonometric expressions that is true for all values of the variable for which both sides are defined.
Identities relating a function of $x$ to its cofunction of $\frac{\pi}{2} - x$, e.g. $\sin x = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)$.
The paired function: sine–cosine, tangent–cotangent, secant–cosecant.

formulas.name: Cofunction identities
formulas.meaning: Also csc x = sec(π/2 − x), sec x = csc(π/2 − x), cot x = tan(π/2 − x).

workedExamples.title: Cofunction evaluation
steps: $\frac{3\pi}{14}$ is in quadrant I. Write it as $\frac{\pi}{2} - a$: $a = \frac{7\pi}{14} - \frac{3\pi}{14} = \frac{4\pi}{14} = \frac{2\pi}{7}$.

workedExamples.title: Using a π-identity
steps: Check signs: $\frac{10\pi}{9}$ is in QIII (cos negative ✓); $\frac{11\pi}{18}$ is in QII (sin positive ✓).

workedExamples.title: Finding an angle
workedExamples.problem: Given $\csc a = \sec 0.75$ and $a$ in the second quadrant, find $a$.
steps: $\csc$ is positive in quadrant II, and $\csc(\pi - a_1) = \csc a_1$.

workedExamples.title: Deriving an identity with the unit circle
workedExamples.problem: Show that $\tan(\pi - x) = -\tan x$ for $x$ in quadrant I.
steps: $P(\cos x, \sin x)$; reflect in the $y$-axis to get the point at angle $\pi - x$: $(-\cos x, \sin x)$.

workedExamples.problem: Find an exact $a$ such that $\sec a = \csc 3a$.

misconceptions.fact: Trig functions do not distribute over subtraction. $\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos x$; e.g. $x = \frac{\pi}{3}$: $\cos\frac{2\pi}{3} = -\frac12$, but $\cos\pi - \cos\frac{\pi}{3} = -\frac32$.
$\cos(x - \pi) = -\cos x$ — subtracting a half turn flips the point to the opposite side of the circle.

misconceptions.myth: Graphs that look the same prove an identity.
misconceptions.fact: Graphs can *suggest* or *verify* equivalence over a window, but a proof needs algebra or geometry valid for all $x$.

misconceptions.myth: Shifts by π change sin to cos.
misconceptions.fact: Only $\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $\frac{3\pi}{2}$ switch to the cofunction. $\pi$ and $2\pi$ keep the same function.

realWorld.title: Aviation
realWorld.body: The radius of a banked turn is $r = \frac{v^2}{g\tan\theta}$: at 50 m/s and a bank of $\frac{\pi}{6}$, $r = \frac{2500}{9.8\tan\frac{\pi}{6}}\approx 442$ m.

realWorld.title: Computer hardware
realWorld.body: Graphics chips save time by replacing a calculation like $\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)$ with the already-computed $\sin x$.

realWorld.title: A broken calculator key
realWorld.body: If the sin key fails, $\sin\frac{9\pi}{13} = \cos\left(\frac{9\pi}{13} - \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \cos\frac{5\pi}{26}$ can be found with the cos key.

practice.question: Given $\cot\frac{2\pi}{5} = \tan z$, express $\frac{2\pi}{5}$ as $\frac{\pi}{2}$ minus an angle and find $z$.
If $\sin x = \cos\frac{3\pi}{11}$ and $x$ is in the second quadrant, find $x$.
practice.hint: First-quadrant solution, then use $\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x$.

practice.question: Use the unit circle to write $\sec(2\pi - x)$ and $\csc(\pi + x)$ in terms of $x$.
Find exact $b$ if $\csc\left(6b + \frac{\pi}{8}\right) = \sec\left(2b + \frac{\pi}{8}\right)$.
practice.hint: Arguments of a cofunction pair add to $\frac{\pi}{2}$.

summary: Equivalent expressions have equal values for all defined angles; an identity states this equality.
Cofunction identities: a function of $x$ equals its cofunction of $\frac{\pi}{2} - x$.
Unit-circle symmetries give identities for $\frac{\pi}{2} \pm x$, $\pi \pm x$, $\frac{3\pi}{2} \pm x$, $2\pi - x$.
Rule of thumb: $\pi$ and $2\pi$ keep the function, $\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $\frac{3\pi}{2}$ switch to the cofunction; the quadrant decides the sign.
Use these identities to evaluate ratios, find unknown angles, and simplify formulas; use graphs to verify.

questions.text: You are given $\sin\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }\approx {{sin(pi/n):4}}$. Without evaluating any other trig function on a calculator, determine the following to four decimal places. Show the equivalent expression you use for each.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $\frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{ {{n}} } = \frac{ ({{n}}-2)\pi}{ {{2*n}} }$, so $\cos\frac{ {{n-2}}\pi}{ {{2*n}} } = \sin\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }\approx {{sin(pi/n):4}}$ (cofunction identity).

(b) $\frac{ {{n+2}}\pi}{ {{2*n}} } = \frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$ and $\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + x\right) = -\sin x$, so the value is $\approx {{-sin(pi/n):4}}$.

(c) $\frac{ {{n+1}}\pi}{ {{n}} } = \pi + \frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$ and $\sin(\pi + x) = -\sin x$: $\approx {{-sin(pi/n):4}}$.

(d) $\frac{ {{n-1}}\pi}{ {{n}} } = \pi - \frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$ and $\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x$: $\approx {{sin(pi/n):4}}$.

questions.text: Given that $\csc a = \sec {{b}}$ and that $a$ lies in the first quadrant, use a cofunction identity to determine $a$ to two decimal places. Then find the second-quadrant angle with the same cosecant.
questions.modelAnswer:
Cofunction identity: $\sec b = \csc\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - b\right)$. So $a = \frac{\pi}{2} - {{b}}\approx {{pi/2-b:3}}$.

Cosecant (like sine) is positive in quadrant II and $\csc(\pi - a) = \csc a$, so the second angle is $\pi - {{pi/2-b:4}}\approx {{pi/2+b:3}}$.

questions.text: Use a right triangle $ABC$ with $\angle B = \frac{\pi}{2}$ and $\angle A = x$ to derive the cofunction identities $\sin x = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)$ and $\tan x = \cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)$. Explain why they are called cofunction identities.
questions.modelAnswer:
The angles add to $\pi$, so $\angle C = \pi - \frac{\pi}{2} - x = \frac{\pi}{2} - x$.

Label sides $a$ (opposite A), $c$ (opposite C) and hypotenuse $b$.

$\sin x = \frac{a}{b}$, and for angle C the side $a$ is adjacent: $\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = \frac{a}{b}$. So $\sin x = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)$.

$\tan x = \frac{a}{c}$ and $\cot C = \frac{\text{adj}}{\text{opp}} = \frac{a}{c}$, so $\tan x = \cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)$.

They relate a function of an angle to its **co**function (cosine = "complement's sine") of the **co**mplementary angle.

rubric.point: Correct side ratios for sin x and cos C
Correct ratios for tan x and cot C

questions.text: Use the unit circle and a rotation of $\frac{\pi}{2}$ to show that $\cos\left(x + \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = -\sin x$ and $\sin\left(x + \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \cos x$, where $x$ is in the first quadrant. Then deduce an expression for $\tan\left(x + \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$.
questions.modelAnswer:
$P(\cos x, \sin x)$ is on the unit circle. A counterclockwise rotation of $\frac{\pi}{2}$ about the origin maps $(a, b)\to(-b, a)$, so $P' = (-\sin x, \cos x)$. The triangles formed with the $x$-axis are congruent, so the coordinates swap with a sign change.

$P'$ is on the terminal arm of $x + \frac{\pi}{2}$, so $\cos\left(x + \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = -\sin x$ and $\sin\left(x + \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \cos x$.

$\tan\left(x + \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \frac{\cos x}{-\sin x} = -\cot x$.

rubric.point: Correct image under rotation with justification
Matches coordinates to conclude both identities

questions.text:
Write each expression in terms of a trig function of $x$ alone, and justify each with the unit circle or the memory strategy (function switch + quadrant sign).

(a) $\cos(2\pi - x)$ (b) $\tan(\pi + x)$ (c) $\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} - x\right)$ (d) $\sec(\pi - x)$ (e) $\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + x\right)$
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $2\pi$ keeps cos; $2\pi - x$ is in QIV where cos is positive: $\cos x$.

(b) $\pi$ keeps tan; QIII, tan positive: $\tan x$.

(c) $\frac{3\pi}{2}$ switches sin→cos; QIII, sin negative: $-\cos x$.

(d) keeps sec; QII, sec negative: $-\sec x$.

(e) switches cot→tan; QII, cot negative: $-\tan x$.

questions.text:
Given $\tan\frac{4\pi}{9}\approx 5.6713$, determine each value to four decimal places without using a calculator. Justify with an identity.

(a) $\cot\frac{\pi}{18}$ (b) $\tan\frac{13\pi}{9}$ (c) $\tan\frac{5\pi}{9}$

rubric.point: (c) identity and value with correct sign

questions.text: A pilot flying at {{v}} m/s banks the aircraft at an angle $\theta$. The radius of the turn is $r = \frac{v^2}{g}\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right)$, where $g = 9.8$ m/s².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the formula simplifies to $r = \frac{v^2}{g\tan\theta}$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the radius of the turn when $\theta = \frac{\pi}{ {{k}} }$, to the nearest metre.

parts.label: c
parts.text: How does increasing the bank angle affect the radius? Explain.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) By the cofunction identity, $\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = \cot\theta = \frac{1}{\tan\theta}$, so $r = \frac{v^2}{g\tan\theta}$.

(b) $r = \frac{ {{v}}^2}{9.8\tan\frac{\pi}{ {{k}} }}\approx {{v^2/(9.8*tan(pi/k)):3}}$ m.

(c) A steeper bank (larger $\theta$) makes $\tan\theta$ larger, so $r$ is smaller — a tighter turn.

rubric.point: Explains effect of larger bank angle

questions.text: Determine an exact value of $a$ such that $\sec a = \csc({{m}}a)$, where both angles are acute. Explain your reasoning and check your answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Value of a (exact; enter a decimal approximation here)

questions.modelAnswer:
Cofunction identity: $\csc y = \sec\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - y\right)$, so the arguments of a sec–csc pair add to $\frac{\pi}{2}$:

$a + {{m}}a = \frac{\pi}{2}\ \Rightarrow\ {{m+1}}a = \frac{\pi}{2}\ \Rightarrow\ a = \frac{\pi}{ {{2*(m+1)}} }$.

Check: $\sec\frac{\pi}{ {{2*(m+1)}} }\approx {{1/cos(pi/(2*(m+1))):4}}$ and $\csc\frac{ {{m}}\pi}{ {{2*(m+1)}} }\approx {{1/sin(m*pi/(2*(m+1))):4}}$ ✓

rubric.point: Sets sum of arguments equal to π/2

questions.text: Determine an exact value of $b$ such that $\csc\left({{p}}b - \frac{\pi}{8}\right) = \sec\left({{q}}b + \frac{\pi}{8}\right)$.
questions.modelAnswer:
For the cofunction pair, the arguments add to $\frac{\pi}{2}$:

$\left({{p}}b - \frac{\pi}{8}\right) + \left({{q}}b + \frac{\pi}{8}\right) = \frac{\pi}{2}\ \Rightarrow\ {{p+q}}b = \frac{\pi}{2}\ \Rightarrow\ b = \frac{\pi}{ {{2*(p+q)}} }\approx {{pi/(2*(p+q)):4}}$.

Check: LS $= \csc\left({{p}}b - \frac{\pi}{8}\right)\approx {{1/sin(p*pi/(2*(p+q)) - pi/8):4}}$, RS $= \sec\left({{q}}b + \frac{\pi}{8}\right)\approx {{1/cos(q*pi/(2*(p+q)) + pi/8):4}}$ ✓

rubric.point: Recognises arguments must sum to π/2

questions.text: Charmaine's sine key is broken. Describe two different methods she could use to evaluate $\sin\frac{9\pi}{13}$ using only the cos key (and arithmetic). Show that both give the same value.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Method 1:** $\sin x = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)$: $\sin\frac{9\pi}{13} = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{9\pi}{13}\right) = \cos\left(-\frac{5\pi}{26}\right) = \cos\frac{5\pi}{26}$ (cosine is even).

**Method 2:** $\sin\left(x + \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \cos x$ with $x = \frac{9\pi}{13} - \frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{5\pi}{26}$, giving $\cos\frac{5\pi}{26}$ again; or use $\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x$ to get $\sin\frac{4\pi}{13}$, then $\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{4\pi}{13}\right) = \cos\frac{5\pi}{26}$.

Also possible: $\sin x = \sqrt{1 - \cos^2 x}$ (positive since $\frac{9\pi}{13}$ is in QII).

Value: $\cos\frac{5\pi}{26}\approx 0.8230$.

questions.text: A student claims that $\cos(x - \pi) = \cos x$ for all $x$. Use the unit circle to decide whether the claim is true. If it is false, give a counterexample and state the correct identity.
questions.modelAnswer:
Subtracting $\pi$ rotates the point $(\cos x, \sin x)$ by a half turn to $(-\cos x, -\sin x)$. So $\cos(x - \pi) = -\cos x$ — the claim is false (except where $\cos x = 0$).

Counterexample: $x = 0$: $\cos(-\pi) = -1$ but $\cos 0 = 1$.

rubric.point: Uses the half-turn on the unit circle

questions.text: Given $\sin x = \cos\frac{ {{k}}\pi}{ {{n}} }$ where $x$ lies in the second quadrant, determine $x$ exactly.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first-quadrant solution is $\frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{ {{k}}\pi}{ {{n}} }$ (cofunction identity). Since $\sin(\pi - y) = \sin y$ and sine is positive in quadrant II,

$x = \pi - \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{ {{k}}\pi}{ {{n}} }\right) = \frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{ {{k}}\pi}{ {{n}} } = \frac{ ({{n}} + {{2*k}})\pi}{ {{2*n}} }\approx {{pi/2 + k*pi/n:4}}$.

rubric.point: Uses sin(π − y) = sin y for quadrant II

questions.text:
Simplify each expression fully. State each identity you use.

(a) $\sin(\pi - x) + \sin(\pi + x)$

(b) $\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\csc x$

(c) $\tan(2\pi - x)\cot(\pi - x)$

(d) $\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + x\right) - \cos(\pi - x)$
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $\sin x + (-\sin x) = 0$.

(b) $\sin x\cdot\frac{1}{\sin x} = 1$.

(c) $(-\tan x)(-\cot x) = \tan x\cot x = 1$.

(d) $\cos x - (-\cos x) = 2\cos x$.

questions.text: Describe how you would use graphing technology to *verify* that $\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} - x\right) = -\sin x$. Explain what you would expect to see, why the graphs alone do not *prove* the identity, and how the unit circle could be used to prove it.
questions.modelAnswer:
Set the calculator to radian mode. Enter $Y_1 = \cos(3\pi/2 - x)$ and $Y_2 = -\sin x$ with a heavier line style; use a window such as $-2\pi\le x\le 2\pi$, $-1.5\le y\le 1.5$. If equivalent, $Y_2$ traces exactly over $Y_1$. A table of values should also match.

```plot
f: cos(3*pi/2 - x)
f: -sin(x) | dashed
domain: -6.3, 6.3
range: -1.5, 1.5
xticks: pi
```

The graph shows only a finite window and limited precision, so it cannot show equality for **all** $x$. A proof: for $P(\cos x, \sin x)$, the angle $\frac{3\pi}{2} - x$ gives the point $(-\sin x, -\cos x)$ (reflect $P$ in the line $y = x$ to get $(\sin x, \cos x)$, then rotate by $\pi$). Its $x$-coordinate is $-\sin x$, so $\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} - x\right) = -\sin x$.

rubric.point: Correct technology procedure (radian mode, two functions, suitable window)
Explains why graphs are not a proof

questions.text: Determine an exact value of $c$ such that $\cot\left({{p}}c - \frac{\pi}{4}\right) - \tan\left({{q}}c + \frac{\pi}{4}\right) = 0$.
questions.modelAnswer:
$\cot A = \tan B$ when $A + B = \frac{\pi}{2}$ (cofunction identity). So

${{p}}c - \frac{\pi}{4} + {{q}}c + \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{2}\ \Rightarrow\ {{p+q}}c = \frac{\pi}{2}\ \Rightarrow\ c = \frac{\pi}{ {{2*(p+q)}} }\approx {{pi/(2*(p+q)):4}}$.

Check: $\cot\left({{p}}c - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\approx {{1/tan(p*pi/(2*(p+q)) - pi/4):4}}$ and $\tan\left({{q}}c + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\approx {{tan(q*pi/(2*(p+q)) + pi/4):4}}$ ✓

rubric.point: Rewrites as cot A = tan B

questions.text: Explain a reliable strategy for writing any expression of the form $f\left(\frac{k\pi}{2} \pm x\right)$ (where $f$ is one of the six trig functions and $k$ is 1, 2, 3 or 4) in terms of a function of $x$. Illustrate your strategy with $\sec\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} + x\right)$ and $\cot(\pi - x)$.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. If $k$ is even ($\pi$, $2\pi$), keep the same function; if $k$ is odd ($\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\frac{3\pi}{2}$), change to the cofunction.
2. Treat $x$ as a small positive angle, find the quadrant of $\frac{k\pi}{2}\pm x$, and attach the sign that the **original** function has in that quadrant (CAST).

$\sec\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} + x\right)$: odd → csc; angle in QIV where sec (like cos) is positive: $\csc x$.

$\cot(\pi - x)$: even → cot; QII where cot is negative: $-\cot x$.

rubric.point: Rule for the sign using quadrant of original function
